label: Chapter 7: Two Wars, Expo 58 and the Capital of Europe, 1914 to 1989

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: We left off in the summer of 1914, with Germany's plan requiring an army to march through Belgium.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the fourth of August, 1914, German troops crossed into Belgium.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The German government had offered the Belgians a deal: let our army pass through your country to attack France, and you will be spared.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: King Albert the First refused.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Belgians, he said, would defend their independence.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the neutrality treaty?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Germany's chancellor dismissed the treaty that Germany itself had signed, the treaty of 1839, as nothing more than a scrap of paper.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Britain, which had guaranteed it, declared war.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: How did Brussels fare?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Belgian army fought hard, and the German advance was slowed, but it couldn't be stopped.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the twentieth of August, German troops marched into Brussels, which had been declared an open city to spare it from destruction.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The occupation would last more than four years, with curfews, requisitions, food shortages, and harsh punishments.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the king?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: King Albert and what was left of the Belgian army held a narrow strip of land in the far west of the country, along the river Yser, for the entire war.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The occupation gave Brussels one of its best-known heroines, Edith Cavell.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: An English nurse who had come to Brussels in 1907 to run a training school for nurses.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: When the war began, she and a network of Belgian and French helpers began hiding Allied soldiers who had been cut off behind enemy lines, and guiding them across the border into the neutral Netherlands.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: She's believed to have helped about two hundred men escape.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And she was caught.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In August of 1915, the Germans arrested her.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: She openly admitted what she had done.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: She was tried, sentenced to death, and on the twelfth of October, 1915, shot by a firing squad, in the early morning, at a shooting range in the Brussels suburb of Schaerbeek.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Her execution caused an outcry around the world.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: What she said the night before is remembered.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: She told a chaplain that patriotism was not enough, and that she must have no hatred or bitterness toward anyone.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: When does the war end for Brussels?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In November of 1918, and on the twenty-second of that month King Albert rode into a liberated Brussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The next two decades were a time of recovery and glamor.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Art Deco buildings appeared across the city.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The great Palais des Beaux-Arts, designed by Victor Horta, opened in 1928.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the science.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1927, the fifth Solvay Conference gathered in Brussels, where the leading scientists of the age, including Einstein, Bohr, Marie Curie, Heisenberg, and Schrödinger, debated the strange new science of quantum mechanics.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the arts?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The surrealist painter René Magritte lived and worked in the city.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And a young Brussels cartoonist named Georges Remi, who signed his work Hergé, published the first adventure of a young reporter with a quiff of red hair in a children's supplement of a newspaper in January of 1929.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Tintin.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Belgium's comic strip tradition, which would make Brussels a world capital of the form, had begun.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Then the Germans came again.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the tenth of May, 1940, they invaded Belgium.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: King Leopold the Third, who had succeeded his father Albert, surrendered the army eighteen days later, against the wishes of his government, which went into exile in London.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The king stayed in Belgium as a prisoner.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That decision would split the country for years afterward.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: What was the occupation like?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Four years. Resistance networks sprang up, helping Allied airmen to escape, hiding Jewish children, and publishing underground newspapers.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But the occupation was brutal.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Tens of thousands of Belgians were sent to forced labor in Germany, and about twenty-five thousand Jews, most of them from Brussels and Antwerp, were deported to the death camps through a transit camp in the city of Mechelen.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: How many survived?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Only a small fraction. Many Belgian families risked their lives hiding Jewish neighbors.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And liberation?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the third of September, 1944, British tanks of the Guards Armoured Division rolled into Brussels to scenes of overwhelming joy.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Compared to many other European cities, Brussels came through the war relatively unscathed.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Its buildings were mostly intact, and its position in the center of Western Europe was about to become its destiny.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But first there was the question of the king.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: After the war, many Belgians, especially in Wallonia and in Brussels, wanted to punish Leopold the Third for his surrender and for some of his actions during the occupation.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Others, mostly in Catholic Flanders, defended him.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1950, a referendum showed that a majority of Belgians wanted him back, but the split followed the language line almost perfectly: strong support in Flanders, and a majority against him in Wallonia and in Brussels.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And it turned violent.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Strikes, riots, and violence followed.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1951, Leopold abdicated in favor of his twenty-year-old son, Baudouin, to calm the country.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was an early sign of how deeply the language divide could cut.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Meanwhile Belgium changed course on neutrality.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It became a founding member of NATO in 1949 and of the European Coal and Steel Community in 1951.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And a Belgian socialist politician, Paul-Henri Spaak, became one of the leading architects of European unity.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1955 and 1956, Spaak chaired the committee that wrote the report that led to the Treaties of Rome of 1957, creating the European Economic Community, the ancestor of today's European Union.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And that's how Brussels got the Commission.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: When the new community needed a home for its executive, the Commission, it was set up in Brussels in 1958, intended as a temporary arrangement.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It never left.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That same year, there was the world's fair.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Expo 58, the first world's fair after the Second World War, opened in April on the Heysel plateau, on the northern edge of the city, and it was meant to show a confident new age of science and peace.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The pavilions of the United States and the Soviet Union stood across from each other, in the middle of the Cold War.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the Atomium.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The most striking structure of all: a giant model of an iron crystal, magnified about a hundred and sixty-five billion times, made of nine shining steel spheres linked by tubes, rising a hundred and two meters into the air.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was supposed to be demolished after the fair, but Brusselers loved it too much.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's now the most recognizable symbol of the city.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Then 1960, and the end of an empire.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the thirtieth of June, 1960, the Belgian Congo became independent.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: At the ceremony, King Baudouin praised Belgium's colonial work, and Patrice Lumumba, the first prime minister of the new country, gave an angry reply about the humiliations and brutality of colonial rule.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And what happened to Lumumba?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Within months, the Congo collapsed into crisis, and in January of 1961, Lumumba was murdered.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Decades later, a Belgian parliamentary commission concluded that Belgian officials bore a moral responsibility for his death, and the Belgian government apologized in 2002.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 2022, Belgium returned a tooth, a relic of his remains, to his family.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The nineteen-sixties are when Brussels starts to look like the capital of Europe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1967, NATO moved its political headquarters from Paris to Brussels, after the French president, Charles de Gaulle, withdrew France from the alliance's military command.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The European Commission moved into a huge, star-shaped office building called the Berlaymont, finished in 1967.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A whole district of offices spread across the eastern side of the city, around the Rue de la Loi.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But the building boom had a cost.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the nineteen-sixties and seventies, developers and the government tore down entire neighborhoods and many fine old buildings to make room for offices, highways, and towers.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: One of the most painful losses was Victor Horta's Maison du Peuple, a masterpiece of Art Nouveau, demolished in 1965 despite protests.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And there's a word for it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Bruxellisation, meaning the careless, speculative destruction of a historic city.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: By the late nineteen-sixties, citizens' groups fought back and began to protect the old districts.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The metro opened in 1976, and the city started, slowly, to be more careful with its past.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And all the while, language politics was getting hotter.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1962 and 1963, Belgium fixed a border between its Dutch-speaking and French-speaking areas, and Brussels was left as a bilingual island inside Flemish territory.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1968, the great Catholic university in Leuven split in two, along language lines.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the constitution followed.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Over the next two decades, a series of constitutional reforms gradually turned Belgium from a centralized country into a federation of regions and language communities.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1989, the third region took shape: the Brussels-Capital Region, made up of nineteen municipalities, officially bilingual.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1993, Belgium formally became a federal state.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: How would someone see this chapter?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Take the metro to Schuman station.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Walk out and you'll face the Berlaymont, with its star-shaped wings, the headquarters of the European Commission.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Nearby is the Cinquantenaire park, where Leopold the Second's arch stands.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And if you have time for a trip to the north end of the city, the Atomium is still there, with a view from the top sphere over the whole region.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: In the final chapter, we come to the Brussels of today.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Which is a lot to take in.
